transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic? What's been going on that made you decide to come see me?

Well... I guess I'm here because my daughter wanted me to come. I just... I don't really have the push for things anymore. I used to go to choir, do some quilting... visit with folks. But now, I mostly just sit at home. I keep the TV on low. I know people expect me to show up, but... I just don't have it in me.
When did you first notice that you stopped having the energy and interest in doing these activities like choir and quilting?
I suppose... it's been a while. Since I retired from the school office. That was a little over two years ago. It just... sort of built up since then.
Before you retired two years ago, have you ever had periods in your life where you felt this way—where you lost interest in things you normally enjoyed and didn't have the energy to do them?
No... I don't think so. I always just... did what I needed to do. Went to work, took care of things. I don't remember feeling quite like this back then.
When you retired two years ago, was that something you wanted to do, or did it feel like something that happened to you that you didn't choose?
I guess... it was just time. I was old enough, so I stopped. Nobody made me do it, if that's what you're asking. I just... filled out the papers and that was it.

When you first retired and stopped working, did these feelings of not having the push and losing interest start right away, or did they develop gradually over weeks or months after you stopped working?
I don't really know. I didn't keep track of it. I just... I couldn't say if it was right away or not. I didn't really notice exactly when it started.

Looking back even further—say, in your 40s or 50s before you retired—did you ever go through a time, even a brief one, where you felt down or depressed, lost interest in things, or struggled to get going?
No... I don't think so. I was just working back then. I didn't really have time to sit around and think about... how I felt. I just got up and did what I had to do every day.
Since you retired two years ago, has there been any particular event or major change—besides just stopping work—that happened around the time these feelings started or got worse?
No. Not really. Just... stayed home. Nothing else happened.
Since you retired two years ago, have there been any times when you felt a bit better—when you had more energy or felt more like doing things—or has it pretty much stayed the same the whole time?
No... I think it's mostly just been the same. I haven't really noticed feeling any different.
Have you ever had a period of several weeks or more where you felt sad, hopeless, or down—even if you didn't call it depression at the time?
No... I don't think so. I don't really... focus on that sort of thing. I just go about my day.
Even if you didn't call it depression, have you ever had a stretch of time—maybe a few weeks or longer—where you felt like life wasn't worth much, or where things just felt dark or pointless?
No... I don't really get like that. I just... wake up and do what I need to do. It doesn't feel dark, just... quiet, I guess. I don't really think about it being pointless.

Around the time you retired two years ago, or since then, have you had any serious medical problems—like a stroke, heart attack, head injury, surgery, or been diagnosed with a new medical condition—or started taking any new medications?
No... nothing like that. I haven't been to a regular doctor in a while. I don't take any pills. Just... healthy enough, I suppose.
Have you noticed any changes in your memory, or do you find it harder to concentrate or make decisions than you used to before you retired?
No... not really. I remember things fine, I think. I don't... I don't really have to make a lot of big decisions anyway these days. So it's just about the same as it always was.

I want to go back to when you were working—say in your 30s or 40s. During those years, did you ever have a time, even if it lasted just a few weeks, where you felt less interested in things, or where you didn't feel like socializing or doing hobbies like you normally did?
No... I don't think so. I just went to work and came home. I never really had many hobbies anyway. Just... kept to myself mostly. It was just normal.
Before you retired two years ago, did you ever go through a period—even just a few weeks—where you felt less motivated, moved slower than usual, or felt tired more easily than you normally did?
No... I don't think so. I just... I always just did my work. I didn't really notice being slower or anything. Just got through the day.
In the two years since you retired, have you had any weeks where you felt sadder than usual, cried more than normal, or felt like things were more hopeless than they are now?
No... I don't get sad like that. I'm not really much of a crier, anyway. Things are just... they just are what they are. I'm fine.

I want to make sure I have this right. In your entire life—going all the way back—have you ever had a time lasting at least two weeks where you felt depressed, or where you lost interest in things you normally cared about, even if you didn't call it depression at the time?
No... I don't think so. I mean, I've just always been the way I am. I never really... got down like you're talking about. I just always kept going.
Have you ever had a head injury, fall, or hit to the head—even if it seemed minor at the time—at any point in your life, particularly around the time you retired or in the years before that?
No... I haven't hit my head. Never had any falls or anything like that. Just... no.
